nodes.title: Give every button an id and its own count
nodes.why: Each button carries a stable id for tracking and for its click handler, plus a count that belongs to it alone, so clicking one button never touches another's number.
nodes.alternative: Keep a plain number[] of counts and identify buttons by their position in the array.
nodes.tradeoff: Objects need an id generator, while positions would point at the wrong button if the list were ever reordered or trimmed.

nodes.title: Hold the whole list in one signal
nodes.why: The @for reads buttons(), and every click hands the signal a new array, so OnPush rendering and anything computed from the list follow each change.
nodes.alternative: A plain buttons array reassigned in the click handler, which renders here because the click marks the view for checking.
nodes.tradeoff: The signal makes every change visible to computed values such as a total; a plain field works only while the click handler is the one thing that changes the list.

nodes.title: Keep the id counter out of the template
nodes.why: nextId only hands out ids and is never displayed, so a private plain field is enough; it starts at 2 because the first button already uses id 1.
nodes.alternative: Make nextId a signal, or derive the next id from the largest id in the list.
nodes.tradeoff: A plain field is the least code; deriving from the list needs no extra state but scans the array on every click and could reuse an id once the last button is removed.

nodes.title: Copy only the clicked button
nodes.why: map returns a new object for the clicked id and the same objects for the rest, so the signal gets a new array while untouched buttons keep their identity.
nodes.alternative: Increment button.count on the existing object and push onto the existing array, which leaves the signal holding the same reference.
nodes.tradeoff: One new array and one new object per click cost nothing at this size; in-place edits would still render after a click but leave a computed total at its old value.

nodes.title: Append a fresh button with the next id
nodes.why: The new button goes on the end of the same new array, so one update both counts the click and grows the list, and @for track button.id gives the new row its own element.
nodes.alternative: Call update twice, once to increment and once to append, or push the new button in a second step.
nodes.tradeoff: One replacement per click keeps the user action in a single write; two writes end in the same list but allocate two arrays and split one click across two steps.
